paper.title: Electrochemical Control of Scholl Reaction: Arenium Cation Versus Radical Cation Pathways
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT The Scholl reaction is a cornerstone method for constructing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, yet its mechanism remains highly debated because arenium and radical cation intermediates are difficult to characterize. Herein, we demonstrate that electrochemical oxidation provides precise mechanistic control: a low‐potential acidic (LPA) condition selectively favors the arenium cation pathway, whereas a high‐potential neutral (HPN) condition promotes the radical cation pathway. While it is often assumed that only one mechanism operates under a given set of chemical oxidation conditions, our results reveal that most substrates can react via both pathways. Dialkoxyphenyl groups are found to facilitate the radical cation pathway, although no general correlation with overall substrate electron richness is observed. This electrochemical control provides the experimental basis to re‐evaluate previously proposed mechanisms for certain substrates. We demonstrate that switching between LPA and HPN conditions yields different products from the same 3,3’‐diphenyl‐2,2′‐binaphthalene substrate, thereby correcting the computational assignment of the corresponding pathways. Additionally, we show that a tetracene‐derived substrate undergoes cyclodehydrogenation through the arenium cation pathway, revising the computationally assigned dication mechanism for this transformation. Collectively, these results establish electrochemistry as a powerful alternative to traditional chemical oxidation, offering unprecedented experimental control to resolve fundamental mechanistic debates about the Scholl reaction.

paper.title: Overcoming the Spin Barrier of Oxygen Redox Chemistry in Lithium–Oxygen Batteries via Metal–Support Magnetic Interaction
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT A major bottleneck for the practical application of lithium–oxygen (Li–O 2 ) batteries is the high overpotential resulting from sluggish kinetics of oxygen redox chemistry. This kinetic limitation can rise in part from the spin‐state transition barriers in converting triplet oxygen ( 3 O 2 ) into peroxide species, alongside the parasitic generation of singlet oxygen ( 1 O 2 ). Here, we demonstrate that metal–support magnetic interactions can effectively overcome this spin barrier. Using palladium (Pd) nanoparticles anchored on ferrimagnetic CoFe 2 O 4 (CFO) substrates as a model catalyst, we reveal that interfacial magnetic coupling restructures the spin and electronic states of Pd sites, generating spin‐polarized active ensembles with optimized adsorption toward oxygen intermediates. This interfacial spin‐electronic effect promotes the conversion of 3 O 2 into peroxide species while suppressing parasitic 1 O 2 evolution during charging, thereby improving the reversibility of oxygen redox chemistry. As a result, the Pd/CFO catalyst achieves a low charging overpotential of 0.05 V and remarkable energy efficiency (91.2%) under spin alignment. This finding establishes metal–support magnetic interaction as a powerful strategy for controlling spin‐dependent oxygen electrocatalysis, providing a general design principle for catalysts involving multi‐site interactions.

paper.title: Mechanistic Investigation and Optimization of a Mixed-Oxide@Alkali Carbonate Redox Catalyst Platform for Enhanced Ethane Oxidative Dehydrogenation
paper.abstract: Abstract Chemical looping oxidative dehydrogenation (CL-ODH) of ethane has emerged as a promising alternative for ethylene production, with the potential to mitigate the environmental and sustainability concerns associated with conventional steam cracking. The main challenge of CL-ODH is the design of active and selective redox catalysts to enhance ethane activation while minimizing the generation of by-products such as COx (CO and CO2). This study employs ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations to investigate the formation and reactivity of oxygen species in mixed metal-oxides@Li2CO3 and Na2CO3 redox catalysts. Estimated reaction free energies are used as thermodynamic descriptors, while the computational insights are supplemented with experimental validations. Our analysis indicates that peroxide (O22–) and •OH radicals provide more favorable thermodynamic driving forces for ethane C–H activation at the outer carbonate surface than monatomic oxygen radical anion (O–) and superoxide (O2–). In addition, mechanistic investigations into COx formation reveal that the product water can interact with peroxide-derived species at the gas–carbonate interface to generate •OH radicals, consistent with prior experimental observations. In Li2CO3, •OH-mediated pathways retain favorable ethane C─H activation thermodynamics while reducing the driving force for selected COx-forming transformations relative to peroxide. These findings provide important mechanistic insights into the design and optimization of mixed-oxide@alkali carbonate core-shell redox catalysts for CL-ODH.

paper.title: Cationic Vacancy Modulates Co Spin State in CoP for pH-Universal and Seawater Hydrogen Evolution
paper.abstract: Abstract Precisely controlling cationic vacancy concentration to tune the spin configuration of metal sites remains a challenge for designing high-performance hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) electrocatalysts. Here, we demonstrated a density functional theory-guided strategy to programmatically engineer cationic vacancies in cobalt phosphide (CoP), enabling targeted modulation of the Co spin state. Theoretical screening identified 8.33% cation vacancies as optimal, which rearranged the unpaired 3d electrons of adjacent Co atoms, lowered the Co magnetic moment to 0.944 μB, and achieved near-thermoneutral hydrogen adsorption free energy (ΔGH* = 0.027 eV). Guided by this prediction, we synthesized CoP-V-0.5 with experimentally determined vacancy concentrations of 10.1% (bulk, ICP-OES) and 7.07% (surface, XPS), which closely approximated the theoretical optimum (8.33%) and validated the DFT-guided design. The optimized catalysts exhibited outstanding HER activity, requiring only 94, 116, and 106 mV to achieve 100 mA cm–2 in 1.0 M KOH, 0.5 M H2SO4, and 1.0 M PBS, respectively, and operated stably for 50 h in alkaline seawater. This work established a theory-guided, spin-mediated paradigm for defect engineering in electrocatalysis.

paper.title: Carbon dioxide as a multifunctional regulator in electrochemical vicinal bromination
paper.abstract: Vicinal dibromination of alkenes is a fundamentally important transformation in organic synthesis, as vicinal dibromides are prevalent motifs in bioactive molecules and serve as indispensable intermediates across chemical synthesis. Despite extensive advances in thermal, photochemical, and electrochemical dibromination, the development of efficient and practical dibromination methods using inexpensive and readily available bromine sources remains highly desirable. In particular, N–H-containing substrates can present additional challenges under oxidative electrochemical conditions because of competing reactions involving the nitrogen functionality. Herein, we report a CO2-mediated electrochemical strategy that enables efficient and chemoselective vicinal dibromination of N–H-containing amino acid-derived alkenes as well as a broad range of functionalized alkenes using NaBr as the bromine source. Mechanistic studies indicate that CO2 plays multiple cooperative roles in this transformation: (i) in situ transient protection of N-H moieties, (ii) formation of carbonic acid with water to replace conventional protic acids, and (iii) lowering of the oxidation potential of bromide ions. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the multifunctional regulatory role of CO2 in the present electrochemical vicinal dibromination system. The authors report a CO2-mediated electrochemical vicinal dibromination, compatible with broad range of alkenes bearing sensitive functional groups, using NaBr as a sustainable bromine source.

paper.title: Diffusion-Selective Modulation Strategy for Enhanced Propane Dehydrogenation via Mixing Inert CHA Zeolite
paper.abstract: Abstract Achieving a high propane conversion in propane dehydrogenation to propylene (PDH) carries tremendous scientific and economic value, particularly if achievable with established industrial units. Here we propose a diffusion-selective modulation strategy driven by large-scale machine-learning computation, where the key to success lies in finding auxiliary materials to drive the PDH reaction forward by enlarging the diffusion-rate difference between H2 and C3 species. This strategy is demonstrated theoretically via high-throughput computation and then validated experimentally through the introduction of inert siliceous CHA zeolites as a diffusion-selective modulator within the catalyst bed. By simply physically mixing CHA with various PDH catalysts, we show that the single-pass propane conversion can increase by 1–5% from industrial space velocities (10 h–1) to significantly higher throughputs (256 h–1), consistently improving performance across multiple reported catalysts without compromising stability. This “plug-and-play” methodology can be directly implemented in existing industrial PDH units without altering either the catalyst formulation or the reactor configuration, providing a readily implementable and scalable route for upgrading current PDH infrastructure.

paper.title: Non-equilibrium modeling of flux through biomolecular condensates
paper.abstract: Cellular biomolecular condensates function far from equilibrium, sustained by continuous influx and efflux of molecular components. Notable examples include the nucleolus, P-bodies, and stress granules, in which regulated molecular transport is essential for their function. Experimental characterization of molecular flux through condensates remains challenging due to limitations in spatiotemporal resolution, making computational approaches a powerful alternative for systematic investigation. Here, we present a computational approach (TRACE) to model molecular transport through biomolecular condensates under non-equilibrium steady-state conditions at residue-level resolution. Using TRACE, we systematically probe physicochemical factors that govern molecular flux through model condensates. We find that protein sequence composition and patterning determine the internal `mesh size' of the condensates, which strongly dictates molecular transport efficiency, and the ballistic-to-diffusive dynamics crossover of the fluxing molecules. We also find that molecule stiffness can enhance their flux by exposing larger surface for intermolecular interactions. Furthermore, we find that modulating host-guest interactions can modulate solubility and friction which jointly governs molecular flux. Finally, we use our framework to show that crosslinking reduces condensate pore size, hindering molecular flux -- consistent with experimental observations of dextran diffusion through nucleolar phases. Collectively, these insights provide a basis for rationally tuning condensate-mediated molecular flux, with potential applications in therapeutics and soft material design.

paper.title: Electron Donor–Acceptor Complex Catalysis in Synthetic Chemistry
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Electron donor–acceptor (EDA) complexes have become powerful platforms for light‐driven radical synthesis. Although stoichiometric EDA photochemistry is now well established, its translation into catalysis is a more recent advance that requires charge‐transfer excitation to be integrated with catalyst regeneration and productive turnover. This review focuses on the design principles that enable EDA complex catalysis, combining fundamental physical–organic concepts with mechanistic criteria for identifying productive catalytic manifolds. Current catalytic approaches are organized into donor‐based, acceptor‐based, and hybrid platforms, with emphasis on how transient catalytic species, medium effects, supramolecular organization, and confined environments facilitate EDA complex formation and expand the range of accessible synthetic transformations. By defining how photoactive donor–acceptor assemblies can be generated, activated, and regenerated within catalytic cycles, this review provides a framework for designing selective and synthetically useful light‐driven catalytic radical processes.

paper.abstract: Abstract Conversion of CO2 into fuels is a potential method to diversify carbon feedstocks and utilize a greenhouse gas. Electrochemical CO2 reduction (eCO2R) is a pathway to convert CO2 into ethylene and CO at mild conditions using renewable electricity. Fuel-grade hydrocarbons can be produced by ethylene oligomerization; however, CO often poisons ethylene oligomerization catalysts, requiring expensive CO removal processes. To integrate the impure intermediate feedstock of CO and ethylene derived from CO2 and the molecular catalysts required for Cn product generation without substantial CO poisoning, optimization of both electrochemical and organometallic catalysis was required. Herein, we demonstrate C4–C28 hydrocarbon production from CO2 and water with CO capture via ethylene-CO copolymerization instead of ethylene purification. For this system, we developed Pd-phosphinosulfonate-borane adduct catalysts that tolerate small quantities of CO while retaining ethylene oligomerization activity, forming internal olefins. The eCO2R performance was optimized to increase the ethylene-to-CO ratio as necessary for efficient conversion to fuels, reaching over 18% ethylene with a 2.4-fold excess over CO under recirculation. Ethylene oligomer formation is achieved with a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 17% and a CO2 conversion (χCO2) of 5%, while the FE and χCO2 toward polymers are 18% and 7%.

paper.title: Reversible dissociation of a sterically distorted dimer of a phosphagermylenylidene
paper.abstract: Accessing heavier analogues of isonitriles remains challenging because inefficient π overlap leads to weak and highly polarized π bonds that strongly favor dimerization or oligomerization. Herein, we report the experimentally observed dimer–monomer equilibrium of a phosphagermylenylidene in solution. Steric protection by a hydrindacenyl ligand renders the dimer highly sterically distorted and only weakly thermodynamically stabilized, enabling reversible dissociation to the monomer. The equilibrium has been studied by variable-temperature nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy in benzene-d6 solution, affording a modest driving force for dimerization (ΔHΘ = 16.26( ± 0.83) kcal mol−1 and ΔSΘ = 3.98( ± 0.26) × 10−2 kcal mol−1 K−1) through van’t Hoff analysis. The transient monomer can be trapped by the weak Lewis base tetrahydrofuran without substantial perturbation of the intrinsic P=Ge bonding. Both the dimer and the weakly coordinated monomer function as phosphagermylenylidene synthons, enabling C ≡ C and Si–H bond activation. These findings demonstrate that weak coordination combined with steric control provides a general strategy for accessing reactive heavier isonitrile analogues while preserving their intrinsic reactivity. Accessing heavier analogues of isonitriles remains challenging because inefficient π overlap leads to weak and highly polarized π bonds that strongly favor dimerization or oligomerization. Herein, the authors report the reversible dimer–monomer equilibrium of a phosphagermylenylidene in solution.

paper.title: Buried Ion-Pairs Reshape Folding Pathways of Artificial Proteins
paper.abstract: Ion-pairs are central charged motifs that control the biological function of several proteins. Yet, the physical principles linked to the formation of ion-pairs during protein folding remain poorly understood. Here, we show that buried ion-pairs of de novo-designed helical bundle proteins reshape the folding pathways by introducing kinetic barriers that are overcome by a hydrophobic collapse linked to packing of the protein core. By combining protein design with co-translational folding studies, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that introduction of a buried ion-pair leads to a shifted folding transition that balances desolvation and electrostatic interactions within the protein and the bulk solvent. Moreover, we find that the folding pathway is sensitive to modifications in non-polar interactions and motifs that electrostatically shield the ion-pair from its surroundings. Our combined findings provide a blueprint for understanding how functional motifs affect protein folding and how mutation of charged networks alter the stability of proteins.

paper.title: NO3– and *H Regulation on CoFe/FeN via Coordination Engineering for Efficient Nitrate Removal and Electroreduction to Ammonia
paper.abstract: Abstract The electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction (NO3–RR) to ammonia shows high potential for balancing the global nitrogen cycle. Owing to facile *NO3 adsorption, nontoxic and inexpensive Fe-based materials are particularly suitable for nitrate reduction. However, generating active hydrogen (*H) on the Fe surface is challenging and inefficient, leading to low Faradaic efficiency (FE) and limited ammonia yield. This study reports that effective modulation of metal–metal and metal–nitrogen coordination in CoFe/FeN-2 by optimizing specific Co/Fe ratios and gas compositions in a two-step approach, which significantly promote the reduction and hydrogenation processes of NO3–RR. In situ characterization and theoretical calculations show that coordination-engineered Co–Fe and Fe–N bonds regulate NO3– and *H adsorption, improve the intrinsic activity of the CoFe/FeN-2 catalysts, and reduce the occurrence of competitive hydrogenation side reactions. Consequently, CoFe/FeN-2, with an optimal FE of 99.05% and ammonia selectivity of almost 100% at −0.68 V vs RHE, has significantly better NO3–RR activity than CoFe/FeN-1 and CoFe. This well-matched two-step method effectively modulates the coordination of iron-based electrocatalysts and provides a new strategy for achieving the design and synthesis of high-performance nitrate reduction electrocatalysts.

paper.title: Hydrogen Isotope Exchange Catalyzed by Pyridine Dicarbene Cobalt Complexes Using Deuterium Gas
paper.abstract: Abstract The catalytic performance of the pyridine dicarbene cobalt complex (iPrACNC)CoPh was evaluated for the hydrogen isotope exchange (HIE) of arenes, heteroarenes, and active pharmaceutical ingredients using D2 gas as the isotope source. The C–H functionalization reaction exhibited a broad substrate scope, tolerated an array of common organic functional groups and enabled the deuteration of a host of sterically accessible C(sp2)–H bonds. The cobalt catalyst was also effective for HIE at low pressures of D2 in polar aprotic solvents. Mechanistic studies support a pyridine dicarbene cobalt(I) aryl complex as the catalytic resting state and a catalytic cycle involving cobalt(I)–hydride-mediated C(sp2)–H activation. Taken together, this work establishes (iPrACNC)CoPh as an effective catalyst for HIE and expands the application of earth-abundant metal catalysis in late-stage isotopic labeling of organic molecules.

paper.title: Engineering the Interfacial Microenvironment to Boost Ethane Dehydrogenation on Ga2O3-Pt Catalysts via Metal Doping Modulation
paper.abstract: Abstract Inverse Ga2O3-Pt catalysts have exhibited better catalytic performance in propane dehydrogenation due to their tunable interfacial electronic properties. This study explores the potential of inverse Ga2O3-Pt catalysts and their single-atom-doped variant (Ga2O3-M/Pt) systems for ethane dehydrogenation using DFT calculations and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations. The results show that Ga2O3-Pt exhibits low ethylene formation activity (0.83 × 102 s–1) and selectivity (84.28%) due to its interfacial sites that weakly and uniformly adsorb hydrogen, impeding the differential regulation of key CH2CH3* intermediate adsorption behavior. Single-atom doping (M = Ti, Co, etc.) creates a Pt–M–O interfacial microenvironment, modulating the electronic structure of interfacial oxygen sites, which enables the effective differential regulation of CH2CH3* intermediate adsorption, thereby enhancing catalytic performance. Among the 14 screened dopants, the Ga2O3-Ti/Pt catalyst emerged as optimal, showing high activity (2.86 × 103 s–1) and selectivity (97.13%) for ethylene formation at the optimal 873.15 K and CH3CH3(g) partial pressure of 0.20 bar. This advantage stems from its moderate p-band center and Ti–O charge transfer, which yield an ideal hydrogen adsorption energy for CH2CH3* regulation. The H* adsorption energy can serve as a descriptor for qualitatively evaluating the activity of CH2CH2(g) formation for a series of Ga2O3-M/Pt catalysts. This work proposes the strategy of “interfacial microenvironment reconstruction to regulate the electronic structure” as a design method for developing high-efficiency alkane dehydrogenation catalysts.

paper.title: Deciphering Interheme Electron-Transfer Pathways in a Diheme Peroxidase from Methane-Oxidizing Bacteria
paper.abstract: Abstract Bis-FeIV-forming enzymes represent an emerging paradigm in high-valent heme iron chemistry, in which two hemes separated by 15–20 Å are both oxidized to the FeIV state. A tryptophan positioned between the two hemes in two out of the three known enzymes to form this state, MauG and MbnH, has been proposed as the dominant pathway for interheme electron transfer. .The third enzyme, BthA, instead has a serine at this position. Here, we used site-directed mutagenesis of Trp113 in MbnH to test whether this tryptophan is uniquely required for interheme electron transfer. Computational pathway analysis identified the possibility of an alternative, noncovalent route mediated by Arg283 and a heme propionate with possible electronic coupling comparable to that of the native tryptophan pathway. Consistent with this prediction, only simultaneous disruption of both the tryptophan and propionate-mediated pathways abolished bis-FeIV formation entirely. Moreover, only mutants capable of forming bis-FeIV retained the ability to turnover substrate, directly establishing this high-valent state as the catalytic intermediate responsible for substrate modification. These results demonstrate that an intervening tryptophan is not required for fast interheme electron transfer, and instead reveal an additional, noncovalent pathway that may be a general feature of diheme peroxidases.

paper.title: A Programmable KillSwitch in NewTAML Catalysts Decouples Oxidative Reactivity from Catalyst Lifetime
paper.abstract: Abstract Bis-amido-bis-sulfonamido, [Fe{4-NO2C6H3-1,2-(NCOCMe2NSO2)2CR1R2}(OH2)]− [2; R1/R2 = H/H (2a), H/CH3 (2b), CH3/CH3 (2c)], are NewTAML (NT) iron(III) oxidation catalysts. Herein we identify and mechanistically characterize a ligand-centered, catalyst-lifetime-controlling site (CR1R2), termed a KillSwitch (KS), that enables balancing technical performance with potential safety constraints in NT/Oxidant process design. Under catalytic conditions, CR1R2 sites containing two or one hydrogen(s), (2a, 2b, respectively), undergo deprotonation to form electron-rich ylides that accelerate NT oxidative degradation. The 2a–c series defines a KS susceptibility gradient arising from differential C–H bond acidities controlling the ylide-forming deprotonation─2a, 2b, and 2c represent high-susceptibility-, intermediate-susceptibility-, and null-susceptibility KS states, respectively, thereby providing substantial catalyst functional lifetime control with 2a < 2b ≪ 2c. Kinetic analysis gives similar 2a–c rate constants for H2O2 activation (kI) and substrate oxidation (kII), while catalyst inactivation rate constants (ki) increase markedly and differentially with increasing pH for 2a and 2b, but remain pH-independent for 2c, which degrades more slowly through a separate pathway. Access to null-KS 2c─essential for testing the KS hypothesis─required a decade-long synthetic effort culminating in the quantitative methylation of deprotonated 2b. The KS is expected to be transferable to other NTs with oxidative reactivities distinct from 2a–c, enabling a new dimension in catalyst design that broadly decouples catalytic oxidative aggression from catalyst lifetime. The KS thus provides a practical, safe, and sustainable by design strategy for balancing technical performances against catalyst lifetimes, should shorter-lived NTs become desirable in response to discoveries of postrelease NT adverse environmental effects.

paper.title: Reaction-based cryo-EM resolves the continuous conformational spectrum of CTP synthase catalysis
paper.abstract: Capturing enzymes under native turnover conditions remains a grand challenge in structural biology. Here, we develop a reaction-based cryo–electron microscopy (cryo-EM) strategy that directly samples Drosophila melanogaster cytidine triphosphate synthase (CTPS) from actively catalyzing mixtures containing only natural substrates and allosteric effectors. By integrating reaction-based sampling with three-dimensional variability analysis, we resolve a continuous conformational spectrum of CTPS during catalysis. This approach visualizes the chemical progression of 4-phosphoryl-uridine triphosphate (4Pi-UTP) formation and reveals a previously unobserved co-occupancy pattern of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and CTP at the reaction end point. Cross-validation with nonhydrolyzable ATP analogs demonstrates that UTP phosphorylation by ATP, rather than mere ATP binding, shifts the conformational ensemble toward more closed states. Our findings establish reaction-based cryo-EM as a framework for resolving chemically annotated conformational ensembles without predefining a single trapped intermediate.

paper.title: Interface‐Induced Growth of Macroscopic, Free‐Standing, and Flexible Monolithic Pure MOF Membrane With Adaptive Porosity
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Membrane‐based separation technologies have emerged as energy‐efficient and environmentally sustainable alternatives to traditional industrial separation processes. However, the development of high‐performance separation membranes faces fundamental material challenges, as amorphous polymeric materials typically exhibit poorly controlled pore size distributions while crystalline porous materials encounter intrinsic difficulties in forming continuous, defect‐free membranes at the macroscopic scale owing to inevitable crystal boundaries. Despite their exceptional structural tunability and separation potential, MOF membranes face fundamental challenges in defect‐free fabrication due to intrinsic crystallinity constraints. Integrating the structural precision of crystalline MOFs with the adaptivity of polymers, we successfully fabricated a macroscopic, free‐standing, and flexible monolithic pure MOF membrane through interface‐induced coordination of Co 2+ with the flexible multidentate amino acid ligand 2,6‐diaminopimelic acid (DAP). The flexible alkyl‐chain backbone suppresses long‐range crystallization and reduces interfacial strain during continuous membrane growth. Locally defined Co–amino‐acid coordination units preserve a framework scaffold, while conformationally flexible alkyl segments impart guest‐responsive latent free volume. The flexible Co‐DAP membrane exhibits guest‐responsive dynamic porosity, in which hydration generates water‐accessible transport pathways that regulate hydrated‐state molecular and ionic transport, enabling osmotically driven water/ion separation through coupled transport and interfacial electrostatic effects under conditions relevant to forward osmosis.

paper.title: Comparative Analysis of Relative Ligand Binding Free Energy Simulation Methods: Amber-TI, GROMACS-NETI, OpenMM-FEP, and BLaDE-MSLD
paper.abstract: Abstract Structure-based drug design has become increasingly important in the pharmaceutical industry for accelerating the discovery of effective drug candidates. In particular, ligand binding free energy serves as a critical metric for predicting drug efficacy during the key stages of hit discovery and lead optimization. Continuous progress has been made in the prediction of ligand binding free energies, but direct comparisons of different methods using the same force field remain challenging due to their unique implementations in different simulation engines. In this study, we present a direct comparison of four popular methodologies (Amber-TI, GROMACS-NETI, OpenMM-FEP, and BLaDE-MSLD) for calculating relative binding free energies (ΔΔGbind) with the same Amber protein and ligand force fields using MolCube Alchemical Free Energy Simulator (MolCube-AFES), which provides an input generation workflow to support ΔΔGbind calculations of all four methods. We used 80 alchemical transformations (among the JACS benchmark set by Wang et al.) and two additional applications to compare the predicted ΔΔGbind from the four methods against experimental measurements. All four methods reproduced experimentally observed trends, with most transformations within ±2 kcal/mol from experiments, and showed broadly comparable accuracy with no statistically significant performance differences across the benchmark data set. These results demonstrate that MolCube-AFES enables controlled, cross-platform benchmarking and show that all four different alchemical free energy methods deliver statistically equivalent accuracy, with method selection guided by workflow requirements such as throughput, portability, and perturbation network design rather than expected differences in performance.

paper.title: V─O─Ti Bridge‐Bond Polarity Boosts Na + Migration in V‐Based Fluorophosphates for Fast Sodium Storage
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Vanadium‐based fluorophosphates are promising high‐energy‐density cathodes for next‐generation sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs). However, the pronounced degradation of Na + diffusion at high voltage hinders their fast‐charging capability. Herein, a Ti 4+ ‐doping‐induced bridge‐bond‐polarity‐driven strategy is proposed to reshape the V electronic structure for facilitating V─O electron exchange. Correspondingly, voltage hysteresis, polarization, and structural distortion at high voltage are suppressed, accompanied by enhanced electronic conductivity. Meanwhile, the polar V─O─Ti bridge bonds expand the dominant one‐ and two‐dimensional Na + transport channels by inducing bridging‐O displacement, further boosting Na + migration capability. Therefore, Na 3 V 1.92 Ti 0.08 O(PO 4 ) 2 F 2 with V─O─Ti delivers high capacities of 121.8 and 62.1 mA h g −1 at 0.1C and 50C, respectively, while maintaining excellent cycling stability. Additionally, the 0.92‐Ah Na 3 V 1.92 Ti 0.08 O(PO 4 ) 2 F 2 //HC pouch cell exhibits 80% capacity retention after 1000 cycles at 1C. At the 9 Ah scale, the pouch cell achieves a high energy density of 154 Wh kg −1 . This synergistic reinforcement strategy driven by bridge‐bond polarity paves the way for sustainable high‐power polyanionic SIBs.

paper.title: The Shear-Bond Descriptor and Universal Machine-Learning Potential Enable Large-Scale Discovery of Negative Thermal Expansion Materials
paper.abstract: Abstract Negative thermal expansion (NTE) materials are crucial for mitigating thermal stresses and designing dimensionally stable components in advanced technologies, yet compounds exhibiting this anomalous behavior remain intrinsically rare. The discovery of novel NTE crystals has traditionally relied on serendipitous empirical observation and physical intuition, severely hindered by the absence of universal design principles. Here, by integrating more than a century of accumulated thermal-expansion data with state-of-the-art machine learning, we identify explainable, macroscopic mechanical descriptors for thermal expansion, namely, the shear modulus (G) and the bonding modulus (Ẽ). These descriptors enable the construction of a universal thermal-expansion landscape based on the shear-bond ratio (G/Ẽ), supporting robust classification between positive thermal expansion (PTE) and NTE materials across diverse structural and chemical spaces. Guided by these universal descriptors and powered by high-throughput, finite-temperature simulations using universal machine-learning interatomic potentials, we theoretically predict 3665 NTE crystals exhibiting wide operating temperature windows. Validating this theory-driven paradigm, the experimental synthesis and characterization of 11 previously unreported compounds directly confirm the robust predictive power and transferability of our framework. These results bridge macroscopic mechanics with microscopic lattice dynamics, transforming the discovery of NTE materials into a systematic, scalable, and data-driven science.

paper.title: Asymmetric enzymatic hydrophosphorylation through O 2 activation
paper.abstract: Enzymatic carbon-phosphorus bond formation is extremely rare in nature, limiting biocatalytic access to phosphorus-containing compounds that are widely used in pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. Here, we report an asymmetric enzymatic hydrophosphorylation through oxygen activation using a repurposed flavin-dependent enzyme. Mechanistic studies revealed that reactive oxygen species are converted into productive phosphorus-centered radicals, followed by radical addition and enzymatic hydrogen atom transfer, achieving high enantioselectivity. The enzyme accommodates diverse phosphorus-hydrogen donors that pose challenges to chemical catalysis, enabling the biosynthesis of valuable phosphorus-containing scaffolds. This work expands the scope of biocatalysis to programmable carbon-phosphorus bond formation and establishes a paradigm for channeling oxygen reactivity in enzymes.

paper.title: De Novo Design of Flavoproteins with Controlled Excited State Dynamics
paper.abstract: Designing photochemical properties in proteins is a frontier challenge in biomolecular design, which, when realised, will open new avenues in catalysis and biomolecular electronics. Here we demonstrate an integrated computational design framework, supported by ultrafast spectroscopy, combining protein design, quantum mechanical/molecular mechanics molecular dynamics (QM/MM MD) and electronic structure calculations, to control flavin excited states in de novo proteins. Iterative design yields FC-4D2, a flavocytochrome with covalently bound flavin and non-covalently bound heme B and Fl-4D2, where the heme-binding site is removed. Both proteins are highly thermostable, and access all physiologically relevant flavin redox and protonation states, while high-resolution X-ray crystallography confirms the near-[A]ngstrom-level accuracy in design. Incorporating QM/MM MD and linear-response time-dependent density functional theory (LR-TDDFT) into the design workflow enables engineering of a flavin-tryptophan charge-transfer variant, Fl-4D2CT, that modifies the flavin absorption spectrum, substantially alters its redox properties and suppresses fluorescence. Ultrafast studies reveal how protein design reshapes the excited state relaxation timescale and mechanism. Our study establishes a modular strategy for programming flavin photochemistry in designed proteins.

paper.title: Chain-Length-Dependent Interactions of Polyethylene Nanoplastics with Human Catalase reveals Size based Nanoplastic Toxicity
paper.abstract: Nanoplastic contamination is increasingly recognized as a biochemical stressor, yet the molecular determinants governing how polymer fragment size dictates protein-level interactions remain poorly understood. Here, we combine molecular docking and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize the interaction of polyethylene (PE) oligomers of increasing length (n = 3, 5, 7, and 14 repeat units) with human catalase, a tetrameric heme enzyme central to cellular antioxidant defense. Single-chain simulations reveal that short PE fragments (3-, 5-, and 7-mer) migrate from an initial domain-connector pose toward a heme-proximal, previously characterized inhibitor-binding site, whereas the 14-mer remains kinetically confined to a peripheral surface site, implicating short-chain PE as a potential catalase inhibitor. In multichain corona systems, backbone dynamics show a non-monotonic, chain-length-dependent destabilization, with the 3- and 5-mer inducing the greatest structural perturbation and the 14-mer best preserving native-like dynamics despite forming an extensive, percolating surface network across all four subunits. MM-PBSA free energy decomposition identifies van der Waals interactions as the dominant thermodynamic driver of binding, while electrostatic surface mapping indicates that cationic surface patches instead govern long-range spatial targeting of PE chains. These findings establish a framework linking nanoplastic fragment size to protein-level toxicity, with direct implications for assessing the biochemical risk of environmentally weathered polyethylene.

paper.title: Deep Generative Prior for First-Order Inverse Optimization
paper.abstract: Inverse design aims to recover system parameters from observed responses, a central challenge in domains such as semiconductor manufacturing, structural engineering, materials science, and fluid dynamics. The absence of explicit mathematical formulations in many systems complicates this task and prevents the use of standard first-order optimization methods. Existing approaches, such as generative models and Bayesian optimization, mitigate these challenges but face notable limitations: generative models often require high-fidelity paired data, while Bayesian optimization depends heavily on surrogate models, leading to scalability issues, sensitivity to priors, and vulnerability to noise. We introduce \textbf{Deep Generative Prior (DGP)}, a new framework that enables first-order, gradient-based inverse optimization with surrogate machine learning models. Formally, DGP constrains the optimization of design parameters through a pretrained prior $G(q)$, such that gradients are propagated via the surrogate forward model $F$, i.e., $\nabla_q \mathcal{L}(F(G(q)), u)$, which enforces optimization along the data manifold induced by $G$. By leveraging pretrained Neural Operators as auxiliary priors, DGP enables stable and effective gradient flow through complex surrogate models. We validate DGP on diverse and challenging inverse design tasks, including {2D Darcy flow} (\textbf{standard}), {2D Navier--Stokes fluid dynamics} (\textbf{ill-posed}), and {semiconductor lithography inverse problems} (\textbf{ill-posed} and \textbf{out-of-distribution solutions}). Across these domains, DGP consistently achieves higher solution quality and efficiency compared to existing methods.

paper.title: Autofocusing molecular simulations for integrative structural biology of broad conformational ensembles
paper.abstract: Integrative structural biology seeks molecular descriptions consistent with complementary experimental measurements. A particular challenge arises for molecules whose broad conformational ensembles resist description by a few representative structures, such as natively unfolded proteins and fluid-phase biomembrane lipids. Although molecular simulations can generate such ensembles, their simultaneous agreement with a large number of experimental constraints is commonly prevented by model inaccuracies. Here we introduce autofocusing as an approach that integrates experimental information by automated finetuning of the physical model generating the ensemble. We demonstrate it for a fluid bilayer of the phospholipid POPC, for which no existing force field has simultaneously reproduced the complete set of 82 NMR C-H bond order parameters. Autofocusing brings all the 82 within experimental uncertainty while preserving agreement with independent small-angle X-ray scattering measurements and retaining or improving agreement with untargeted NMR relaxation rates and effective correlation times, thus supporting its description of membrane structure and dynamics beyond the calibration targets. The resulting simulations challenge a long-standing two-state interpretation of phosphatidylcholine headgroup structure, instead supporting a broad conformational ensemble poorly represented by crystal-derived conformers. These results establish autofocusing as a practical approach to constructing experimentally grounded conformational ensembles while retaining the computational tractability of classical molecular dynamics.

paper.title: The CAHRA Challenge: A Community-Wide Assessment of Cryo-EM Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms
paper.abstract: The ability of cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to interrogate the atomic structure and motion of biomolecules has motivated the development of a wide range of algorithms for heterogeneity analysis. However, evaluating and comparing these methods remains challenging because ground-truth structures are generally unknown for experimental samples. Here, we introduce the 2026 Community-Wide Assessment of Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms (CAHRA), a community-wide challenge centered on three benchmark datasets that probe distinct tasks in heterogeneity analysis. These include (1) compositional heterogeneity arising from mixtures of distinct protein complexes, (2) continuous conformational variability and atomic modeling, and (3) entanglement between molecular conformation and particle pose. We describe the design, construction, and validation of these datasets, as well as their use in the recently completed CAHRA Challenge.

paper.title: Coarse-to-Fine Generation of Multiscale Random Fields via Latent Schrödinger Bridges
paper.abstract: Spatial filtering of random fields arises in the multiscale analysis of random heterogeneous materials and produces hierarchies of fields coupled through fine-scale realizations. Because this upscaling process is non-injective, the coarse-to-fine problem is intrinsically stochastic and involves learning a conditional law from data. This work addresses conditional coarse-to-fine generation in the paired setting, where training observations are hierarchies sharing one fine-scale realization: here, interscale coupling is explicitly prescribed from the observed joint probability law and not inferred from separate marginals. We propose a two-stage framework. The first stage encodes the hierarchy with a functional autoencoder regularized by a diffusion prior, yielding two analytical results. First, we show that the prior implicitly penalizes the trace of the decoder's pullback metric at each encoded point, shaping the latent geometry for downstream transport. Second, we prove that improving the prior's denoising accuracy tightens the bridge drift target: at matched noise precision, the denoising risk provides an upper bound for the bridge's endpoint error. The second stage models the encoded hierarchy as a Schrödinger bridge whose skeleton constraint is the paired joint law. Each refinement interval is localized as a Doob $h$-transform with a Dirac marginal and a terminal law drawn from paired data, giving a simulation-free least-squares regression objective for the drift. Reducing full-history to previous-scale conditioning is characterized as an $L^2$-projection of the drift, with exact recovery under a Markov sufficiency condition on the latent skeleton. Experiments on paired two-phase random fields show that the diffusion-prior representation (i) improves reconstruction fidelity and decoder-geometry conditioning over a quadratic-penalty baseline, and (ii) attains better coarse consistency and distributional agreement for out-of-distribution conditioning states.

paper.title: Tracking Without Linking or Localization: Single-Photon Tracking
paper.abstract: Mobile biological particles, ranging from biomolecules to viral capsids, often diffuse faster than 1m2/s, resulting in severe motion blur in conventional millisecond-scale imaging. Shorter exposures capture faster dynamics, but quantizing the per-pixel signal at such exposures eventually degrades our ability to localize particles at all. In the extreme case of binary (1-bit-per-pixel) output--where moving from 8-bit grayscale to 1-bit corresponds to a 255-fold faster acquisition rate--no existing tracking method applies, since all of them rely on intensity-based localization that binary data cannot supply. We therefore introduce single-photon single-particle tracking (SP2T), a framework that bypasses localization and linking by estimating particle numbers and trajectories directly from the full 1-bit image stack. We demonstrate SP2T on single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) arrays, which deliver microsecond exposures over a large field of view (512x512 pixels) and explicitly account for detector-specific artifacts such as hot and cold pixels. We validate the method against programmed fluorescent bead and organic dye trajectories, and apply it to two biological systems, aerolysin and ganglioside GM1. Together with simulation, these experiments reveal that longer exposures bias diffusion coefficient estimates (by up to 70% for particles diffusing at 5m2/s) and distort jump-distance distributions, underscoring the need for photon-by-photon tracking in fast-diffusion regimes. Evaluating the likelihood on a GPU further delivers more than a 50-fold speedup over a CPU implementation when compared on datasets of the same frame size and number of frames, enabling multiplexed tracking for crowded particles. Together, these advances establish SP2T as a robust, data-efficient route to unbiased particle tracking at microsecond temporal resolution.

paper.title: Sequence-Dependent DNA Base Selection Fidelity: A Kinetics-Based Model and its Validation
paper.abstract: DNA replication achieves error rates as low as 10-9-10-11 per base pair through the combined contribution of base selection, exonuclease proofreading, and mismatch repair. Among those processes, base selection determines the initial level of accuracy and is strongly modulated by local sequence context. Existing models address this dependence either by fitting individual rate constants for each sequence context or by invoking the global template properties, neither of which derives sequence dependence from the underlying thermodynamics and kinetics of base pair formation. Here we present a mechanism for sequence-dependent base selection fidelity, built from two physical properties: nearest-neighbor stacking thermodynamics and directional kinetic asymmetry. The model fits the experimentally observed mutation spectra from three mismatch repair-deficient organisms well (r=0.74, 0.70, and 0.63), and predicts that base-selection accuracy varies non-monotonically with temperature in a sequence-dependent manner. Our model, therefore, provides a framework that connects sequence-dependent thermodynamic and kinetic effects during nucleotide incorporation to experimentally observed mutation rates.

paper.title: A modular DNA toolkit for single-molecule biophysics
paper.abstract: Long, customizable DNA molecules are an essential tool for in vitro single-molecule biophysics. Most studies still rely on the {lambda}-phage genome, which has a fixed sequence, a non-uniform GC distribution, and limited options for modification. To overcome these limitations, we developed a modular DNA (ModDNA) toolkit that integrates in silico sequence design with cloning, to create long (up to 100 kb) DNA molecules with entirely user-defined sequences. We used a computational workflow with curated databases to design a motif-depleted sequence backbone, into which any desired sequence can be inserted at any position. Golden Gate assembly then builds these sequences into constructs, which we extend iteratively in defined increments up to 100 kb. We show precise placement of local features, e.g. a fluorophore, a bound protein, and a DNA-origami structure, and illustrate the construct's utility in single-molecule visualization assays, including DNA loop extrusion by human condensin I. ModDNA offers a scalable, sequence-programmable alternative to {lambda}-DNA and other restrictive substrates. More broadly, the motif-aware feature-free design connects single-molecule biophysics to emerging efforts in machine-guided regulatory-sequence design and synthetic-genome engineering, where controlled programmable sequence context is increasingly essential.

paper.title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning from Storage to Inference: Integrating Authenticated Encryption with Fully Homomorphic Encryption
paper.abstract: Abstract Objective Sensitive records may be exposed during storage and remote machine-learning inference. This study evaluated an end-to-end prototype integrating AES-256-GCM authenticated storage with fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) to protect data at rest and during outsourced inference while keeping plaintext inputs and the client’s private FHE key from the inference server. Results A reproducible synthetic dataset of 2,000 household records with ten numeric features was used to train logistic-regression classifiers. The matched plaintext model achieved accuracy 0.9050, F1 score 0.9360 and ROC-AUC 0.9613. Four-, six- and eight-bit FHE models showed comparable predictive performance; the six-bit configuration achieved accuracy 0.9150, F1 score 0.9426 and ROC-AUC 0.9621. Genuine encrypted inference required 30.62–31.04 ms per record. A separate cold-cache end-to-end test evaluated a 504-byte encrypted request server-side in 699.3 ms. Storage testing detected a one-byte ciphertext modification and rejected cross-user access. These findings demonstrate that authenticated storage and FHE inference can be integrated with little observed loss of predictive fidelity, although FHE remains substantially more computationally demanding than plaintext inference.

paper.title: Transcription factor interactions promote binding to non-cognate DNA sites
paper.abstract: Recruitment of transcription factors (TFs) to non-cognate DNA sequences is widely observed, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that, within the nucleosome, Sox2 can bind an Oct4 motif, interact with the Oct4 POU-specific domain, and displace the Oct4 homeodomain. We also observe Sox2 binding at multiple near-canonical and non-canonical DNA sites, with these interactions promoted by a second Sox2 molecule or by nearby nucleosome-bound Oct4. The TF-TF interactions can bridge across DNA gyres, bringing together binding sites that are distant in linear DNA but spatially proximal on the nucleosome. We further find that Sox2 can engage across nucleosomal DNA gyres through loop regions and/or intrinsically disordered segments, providing an additional mode of chromatin binding. Together, our structural and biochemical data reveal how TF-TF interactions change DNA recognition on the nucleosome, enabling binding to non-cognate sequences and expanding the repertoire of pioneer factor interactions on chromatin.

paper.title: A Geometrical Class of Population Growth Models, across Scales and Population Structures
paper.abstract: We develop a general geometrical framework for growth processes in which the growth rate depends exponentially on the number of active growth-supporting components. The framework separates the fraction of active components from the size of the accessible component space, allowing qualitatively different growth laws to arise from the same underlying construction. Bacterial population growth provides an example of a fixed-size component space controlled primarily by activation and deactivation, whereas examples such as human population growth or speciation provide an expanding component space in which interactions between individuals promote further growth. This motivates a Replicative geometrical law, dX/dt= X exp({beta} X^{gamma}), whose exponent characterizes the scaling of the effective growth-supporting component space and is tested against historical human-population regimes and eukaryotic lineage-through-time data. For innovation indicators such as patents and arXiv manuscript submissions, where an existing item need not itself reproduce, the same construction motivates a Direct Geometrical production law without the prefactor X. The framework therefore provides a common description of fixed and expanding component spaces while distinguishing Replicative from Direct Geometrical growth.

paper.title: Structural Basis of Human Kinetochore-Microtubule Coupling by the Ndc80 and Ska Complexes
paper.abstract: Faithful chromosome segregation depends on kinetochore-microtubule attachments that must be load-bearing, dynamic, and tightly regulated. In human cells, the Ska and Ndc80 complexes (SkaC and Ndc80C) cooperate to sustain these attachments, but how they are organized on microtubules and coupled to end dynamics remains unclear. Here, our cryo-EM structure shows that Ndc80C and SkaC form a coupled assembly across neighboring protofilaments. A phosphorylation-sensitive SKA3 tether binds a defined kink in the Ndc80 coiled-coil, positioning SKA1 beside Ndc80C. These two complexes jointly sandwich the -tubulin tail and sense its polyglutamylation state. SkaC recognizes the extended microtubule lattice and, through the SKA3 tether, confers this selectivity onto Ndc80C, enabling Ndc80C tip tracking while strengthening microtubule stabilization. Together, our findings define the structural basis of Ndc80C-SkaC cooperation and uncover a phosphorylation-regulated, polyglutamylation-sensitive, and lattice-state-dependent mechanism for robust and regulated KT-MT coupling during chromosome segregation in mitosis.

paper.title: Structural divergence of G6PD variants shapes red blood cell storage and transfusion performance
paper.abstract: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is the most common enzymopathy, yet how donor alleles shape red blood cell (RBC) storage, transfusion performance, and recipient physiology remains unresolved. Across 13,091 donors, a recalled cohort, donor-recipient data, humanized mice, and a prospective sickle cell disease cohort, variants reduced G6PD abundance, constrained pentose phosphate pathway flux and redox metabolism, and accelerated age-dependent functional decay. Murine A-; RBCs recovered poorly; A-; and Mediterranean RBCs impaired renal oxygenation, especially the latter, which caused greater plasma hemolysis. In humans, A-; units yielded smaller hemoglobin increments, while deficient units reduced allogeneic 51Cr post-transfusion recovery and four-week survival by 8 and 12-percentage-points. NADP;-bound cryo-EM resolved mechanisms: remodeling of the catalytic NADP;-binding region and dimer interface underlies A-; kinetic fragility, whereas Mediterranean S188F exhibits temperature-dependent oligomerization and conformational instability. These findings define an allelic series linking genotype to molecular instability, RBC quality, transfusion performance, and recipient physiology.

paper.title: Transposable element-mediated structural variations shape gene expression and agronomic trait diversity in Brassica napus
paper.abstract: Brassica napus is a globally important allotetraploid oilseed crop with a complex genome and extensive structural diversity that remains incompletely characterized. Here, we present gap-free reference genome assemblies for Zhongshuang 11 (ZS11) and Westar, and assemble six additional accessions. We harmonize gene annotations across 22 genomes and develop BnaScope (https://rgmi.hzau.edu.cn/bnascope), a gene-centric functional genomics platform. Gene-based and graph-based pan-genomes identify 123,107 non-redundant gene clusters and 188,218 structural variants, including 112,417 transposable element-mediated structural variants (TEMSVs). TEMSVs show asymmetric distributions between An and Cn subgenomes and are associated with increased homoeolog expression imbalance, particularly for CDS-TEMSVs. SV-based genome-wide association analyses identify candidate genes underlying seed quality traits, and functional analyses demonstrate that BnaPYRDs negatively regulate seed glucosinolate content. These findings establish structural variation as an important contributor to homoeolog regulation and seed-quality variation in B. napus.

paper.title: Scalable design of fluidic DEMUX/MUX
paper.abstract: Fluidic logic circuits offer a foundation for decentralized onboard control in soft pneumatic robots, enabling their integration into actuator networks to generate complex movements. However, existing fluidic controllers in soft robots face scalability limitations, restricting their ability to handle growing degrees of freedom across sizes while preserving compliance. Here, we present a scalable fluidic control architecture that integrates high-radix demultiplexing with time multiplexing to achieve a high input-to-output ratio and reprogrammable actuation. We incorporate a design method based on dimensionless parameters to preserve comparable valve opening and closing pressure thresholds across different physical scales, thereby maintaining consistent addressing behavior of the demultiplexer after geometric scaling. In addition, structural stretchability enables seamless integration into soft bodies, maintaining reliable control under dynamic deformation without compromising compliance. This hybrid demultiplexer/multiplexer fluidic circuit overcomes key limitations, offering functional scalability, geometric scalability, and physical integrability in a single architecture. Our approach enables autonomous, adaptable soft robots capable of complex, multifunctional motions, functioning as self-contained systems.

paper.title: Resolving Proton Diffusion Kinetics in Electrolytic Hydrogen Evolution
paper.abstract: Abstract Although the hydrogen-bond network within the electrical double layer (EDL) is crucial for proton diffusion in the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), its exact role remains controversial. This debate stems from the experimental difficulty in determining the proton diffusion kinetics during the HER. Here, we employ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) at ultramicroelectrodes to quantify the potential dependence of the non-steady-state diffusion coefficient of protons. By scanning the effect of applied potential and solute species independently, we reconcile contradictory reports by revealing that the determining factor for proton diffusion shifts from hydrogen-bond connectivity to rigidity with increasing polarization. This work provides the principles for regulating proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) in electrocatalysis.

paper.title: Cation-Gated Interfacial Electrocatalysis: Mechanisms and Effects of Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metal Cations
paper.abstract: Abstract Electrolyte cations, long considered inert charge-balancing species, are now recognized as active regulators of electrocatalytic interfaces. This review systematically examines alkali metal cations (Li+, Na+, K+, Rb+, Cs+) and alkaline earth metal cations (Mg2+, Ca2+, Sr2+, Ba2+) in five key reactions: hydrogen evolution/oxidation, oxygen evolution, oxygen reduction, carbon dioxide reduction, and nitrate reduction. We demonstrate that cation effects are reaction-specific, governed by electric double layer structure, interfacial electric fields, local pH, water networks, and intermediate stabilization. Alkali metal cations mainly regulate reactant access, proton transfer, pathway selection, and stability through electric-field modulation, solvation restructuring, intermediate stabilization, and, over longer timescales, catalyst-surface evolution. Hydration characteristics dictate their behavior: weakly hydrated large cations (K+, Rb+, Cs+) enhance local electric fields and stabilize polar intermediates in CO2RR, while strongly hydrated small cations (Li+, Na+) support water dissociation and proton transfer in HER/HOR. Alkaline earth metal cations exhibit chemically coupled interfacial regulation due to higher charge density, stronger hydration, and greater Lewis acidity. These divalent cations facilitate reactions through local pH buffering, water rearrangement, and intermediate stabilization, yet their hydrolysis and precipitation tendencies risk active site blockage and catalyst deactivation, particularly in real electrolytes like seawater and wastewater. By mapping diverse microscopic cation effects onto these five catalytic functions, this review provides a cross-reaction framework for rationalizing apparently contradictory cation trends and identifying the dominant interfacial bottleneck under different conditions. Finally, we highlight future directions in operando characterization, multiscale modeling, multi-ion systems, and electrolyte-catalyst co-design for efficient, selective, and stable electrocatalysis.

paper.title: Cation-Regulated Interfacial Proton Transfer for Enhanced C–C Coupling in Electrochemical CO Reduction
paper.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical CO reduction reaction (CORR) on copper is a prototypical platform for studying C–C coupling toward multicarbon (C2+) products, yet the fundamental factors governing this process remain under debate. Particularly, how electrolyte composition regulates interfacial proton transfer and thereby governs C–C coupling pathways is still unclear. This paper describes the role of alkali metal cations in controlling C–C coupling in CORR by restructuring interfacial water and modulating proton transfer dynamics on Cu electrodes. By varying cation identity (Li+, Na+, K+, Cs+) and concentration, we demonstrate that cations with intrinsic larger ionic radii in the electrolyte shift selectivity toward C2+ products. Combining differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) analysis with in situ surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) and attenuated total reflection surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS) investigations, it is revealed that alkali metal cations with large intrinsic radii have weak hydration shells that disrupt the interfacial hydrogen-bond (H-bond) network and increase the population of cation-coordinated water molecules at the interface, which may serve as more effective proton transfer channels toward surface intermediates. This reconstruction of interfacial water can accelerate *CO hydrogenation, thus promoting the C–C coupling for C2+ production. These findings identify interfacial water as an active regulator of interfacial proton transfer, thereby supporting a mechanistic link between electrolyte composition and C–C coupling pathways. This work emphasizes the importance of the interfacial microenvironment and molecular-level understanding of electrochemical reactions.

paper.title: Single-Water Microsolvation Promotes Proton Sharing in a Neutral Formic Acid–Ammonia Complex
paper.abstract: Abstract Can single-water microsolvation promote proton sharing in a neutral acid–base complex? We address this question for formic acid–ammonia by isolating its monohydrated complex with broadband rotational spectroscopy and interpreting the resolved 14N hyperfine structure with calibrated high-level quantum chemistry. The observed complex is a single dominant HCOOH–NH3–H2O isomer with effective Cs symmetry, in which NH3 remains the primary proton acceptor, while water closes a cooperative hydrogen-bond cycle by accepting from NH3 and donating to the carbonyl oxygen. Rather than simply stabilizing the binary acid–base contact, this water molecule measurably increases its proton-sharing character. A resolved A/E tunneling pattern from NH3 internal rotation supplies the missing orientation needed to rotate the experimental 14N quadrupole tensor into the local ammonia frame, yielding an experimental χzz component and a quadrupole-derived Townes–Dailey ionicity of approximately 26%. High-level structures show the same directional response: O–H elongation, H···N contraction, and O···N contraction relative to HCOOH–NH3. Together, these results show that one water molecule can promote proton sharing in a neutral formic acid–ammonia complex without producing a separated ion pair.

paper.title: Path dependence in alchemical calculations of water chemical potential in aqueous electrolytes
paper.abstract: Accurate calculation of free energies and their derivatives is central to assessing the thermodynamic stability of molecular and particulate systems across length scales. Yet, such quantities can be difficult to compute reliably in strongly interacting systems, such as solutions of ionic species in polar solvents. One important example is the chemical potential of water in aqueous electrolytes, which can be estimated through staged particle insertion by gradually coupling an inserted molecule to its environment. Although the resulting insertion free energy should be independent of the alchemical pathway, the order and manner in which van der Waals and electrostatic interactions are activated can strongly affect convergence and, in some cases, yield inconsistent estimates. Here, we examine this issue by calculating water’s chemical potential in aqueous KCl solutions using eight alchemical insertion pathways that differ in the extent and order of van der Waals and Coulombic coupling. We find that concurrently activating these interactions, particularly in fully coupled and partially end-coupled protocols, can produce chemically implausible insertion free energies. These anomalies arise within the soft-core Hamiltonian from intermediate states in which the inserted water molecule develops strong electrostatic interactions with a chloride ion before sufficient short-range repulsion has been established. In contrast, pathways that activate short-range van der Waals interactions before electrostatics yield more consistent and chemically plausible estimates. These findings demonstrate that practical alchemical calculations in polar and ionic environments can be highly sensitive to pathway design, underscoring the importance of decoupling short-range and electrostatic interactions in staged insertion alchemical protocols.

paper.title: ConSolv: Solvent-Conditional Machine Learning Implicit Solvent Potential
paper.abstract: Abstract Implicit solvent machine learning potentials (MLPs) offer a powerful route to bridging the gap between accuracy and efficiency in molecular simulations. However, existing models have largely focused on aqueous environments, overlooking the diverse and important roles of nonaqueous solvents in areas such as organic synthesis and battery technology. Here, we present ConSolv, a solvent-conditional MLP architecture that explicitly incorporates solvent effects on solute interactions through an attention-based solvent embedding block. By combining experimental solvation free energy data with ab initio data, we train a single implicit solvent MLP that is transferable across 66 common organic solvents. ConSolv outperforms classical explicit solvent methods and selected ab initio implicit solvent approaches across multiple solvation free energy benchmarks, and demonstrates generalization to unseen solvents. Beyond solvation free energies, the model shows close agreement with experimental nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data for γ-fluorohydrin molecules in chloroform. ConSolv’s architecture is readily extensible to broader chemical spaces and alternative training strategies, while its attention-based design supports explainable artificial intelligence (AI) analysis that can help elucidate complex, solvent-dependent molecular interactions.

paper.title: Structural insights into the coupling mechanism of vectorial CO 2 uptake by DAB1
paper.abstract: CO 2 transporters enable bacterial CO 2 -concentrating mechanisms by catalyzing directional hydration of CO 2 , yet the basis of this vectorial carbonic anhydrase (CA) activity remains an open question. We used cryoelectron microscopy to determine the structure of the DAB1 complex from Thermocrinis albus to 2.29 Å, revealing a heterotrimer in which a deeply buried β-CA active site in DabA is structurally coupled to the proton-translocating subunit DabB. Two conformational states define distinct solvent channels for substrate entry and product exit. A suppressor screen identifies mutations that disrupt coupling while retaining CA activity, underlying the importance of conserved residues that link proton translocation to active-site remodeling. These results support a model in which proton-driven conformational changes regulate substrate access to the active site, enabling vectorial CO 2 hydration.

paper.title: Topological control of local electroneutrality in confined electrolytes
paper.abstract: Topology governs finite-size violations of local electroneutrality in confined electrolytes. Within Poisson–Boltzmann theory, we show that this topological control gives rise to a universal hierarchy of deviations in spherical, cylindrical, and planar confinement. We quantify this effect through an electroneutrality deviation ratio that captures the global electrostatic constraints associated with compactness and boundary multiplicity in Ωsph ≃ S2 × [0, δ], Ωcyl≃S1×R×[0,δ], and Ωslit≃R2×[0,δ]. Although local electroneutrality is asymptotically restored in the limit of infinite cavity size, finite-size deviations follow a robust topological hierarchy, being strongest in spherical cavities, weaker in cylindrical confinement, and weakest in planar slits. These results prove that topology is the organizing principle underlying confinement-induced charge redistribution and violations of local electroneutrality constitute a general electrostatic constraint governing overcharging, charge reversal, and long-range charge correlations. More fundamentally, they demonstrate that changing the topology modifies the global electrostatic constraints without altering the local Poisson–Boltzmann equations. As a counterintuitive manifestation of nonlinear confinement in a point-ion model, we report the existence of inside confinement charge reversal in charged hollow cylindrical and spherical nanoparticles. Since physically consistent, more general electrolyte theories must recover the Poisson–Boltzmann description in the appropriate limiting case, the present results establish a benchmark against which topological effects should be assessed beyond the Poisson–Boltzmann description.

paper.title: Electrochemical Nitrogen Reduction to Ammonia with Mesoporous Molybdenum-Carbon Electrocatalysts in a Gas Diffusion Flow Cell
paper.abstract: Abstract Commercialization of electrochemical nitrogen reduction (eNRR) is hindered by limited catalyst performance, the lack of scalable electrochemical cell architectures, and an incomplete understanding of performance-limiting processes. This work aims to address these challenges through a systematic investigation of catalyst composition and microstructure, device configuration, and reaction mechanisms. Molybdenum (Mo) metal single atoms and clusters supported on mesoporous nitrogen-doped carbon were synthesized with tunable pore sizes via a five-second photothermal pyrolysis of a self-assembled bottlebrush block copolymer (BBCP) template. For eNRR, improved Mo dispersion enhanced electrochemical accessibility, while the coexistence of atomically dispersed Mo species and Mo clusters produced a structurally heterogeneous catalytic environment that benefits eNRR. A gas-diffusion electrode (GDE) flow cell was constructed for continuous operation testing; the catalyst–device system achieved a Faradaic efficiency of 21.6% and an ammonia yield rate of 34.7 μg h–1 mg–1. Intermediate pore sizes and balanced electrode wettability promoted effective triple-phase boundary formation and active-site utilization. Electrochemical characterization combined with machine-learning analysis of flow-cell parameters indicated that activation polarization is the dominant loss mechanism, governed primarily by intrinsic active-site kinetics and electrochemically accessible surface area. In contrast, pore size, metal dispersion, and electrode wettability primarily regulate site accessibility rather than mass-transport limitations. Together, these results provide a framework linking catalyst structure, electrode architecture, and kinetic limitations in eNRR flow-cell systems and offer practical design guidelines for advancing scalable eNRR technology.

paper.title: Using large language models to probe the limits of atom-centered structural descriptors
paper.abstract: Mapping an atomic structure to a compact set of geometric descriptors is an essential step in any machine-learning application to atomic-scale modeling. A powerful and widely used approach can be understood as a discretization of the histogram of pair distances, triangles, etc., which results in a hierarchy of symmetry-invariant atom-centered descriptors. Unfortunately, the lower rungs on this hierarchy (two, three, four-body clusters) were found to be incomplete, with symmetry-unrelated pairs of structures having exactly the same descriptors. However, all the “degeneracies” reported so far are resolved by considering larger clusters of neighbors to build the descriptors. We report examples of 3D structures that are indistinguishable even if one considers clusters of up to seven neighbors, and to arbitrary order when considering a practical level of discretization of the descriptors, discovered with the assistance of large language models. The key ingredients in their construction can be traced to results that have been known for decades in different communities: the model was able to find the references and recognize their significance for the problem at hand. We believe that this experiment exposes an extremely fruitful usage pattern for Artificial Intelligence in science: translating results between different communities and application domains, accelerating the process by which serendipitous discoveries in a field become breakthroughs in another.

paper.title: ΔNAzyme: A Foundational QM/MM Δ-Machine Learning Potential for Nucleic Acid Enzyme Catalysis
paper.abstract: Abstract Nucleic acid enzymes (NAzymes), including ribozymes, DNAzymes, and XNAzymes, are programmable biocatalysts that catalyze diverse chemical reactions and provide unique platforms for investigating catalysis and engineering molecular function. Their central roles in biology and evolution, together with emerging applications in biotechnology, synthetic biology, and medicine, have created an urgent need for predictive computational design frameworks. Although multiscale computational enzymology integrating ab initio quantum mechanics can, in principle, provide predictive insight into these systems, current approaches remain computationally prohibitive for large, complex NAzymes and high-throughput design workflows. Machine learning potentials have the potential to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of multiscale modeling approaches, but QM/MM contexts in which the MM environment is highly polarizing remain challenging. Nucleic acid enzymes present a particularly demanding case: experimentally relevant predictions require an accuracy that semiempirical QM/MM methods alone cannot reliably deliver in their often large, highly charged, metal-dependent active sites. Building on the range-corrected QM/MM Δ-machine learning potential (ΔMLP) framework, we develop ΔNAzyme, a foundational ΔMLP for nucleic acid enzyme reactions. We generate a training set of QM/MM simulations spanning diverse nucleic acid enzyme classes, with energies and forces computed at both the reference (DFTB3) and target (PBE0/6–31G*) levels of theory, yielding a correction on top of DFTB3 that recovers PBE0 quality results. We train models using both the Deep Potential and MACE architectures. The MACE model exhibits enhanced transferability, which we attribute to the equivariant, many-body message-passing framework. Free energy profiles from case-study reactions validate ΔNAzyme against target-level results and show that the model supports efficient fine-tuning to new nucleic acid enzyme systems with minimal additional data.

paper.title: Enhanced Sodium Metal Anode Cycling Stability via an Organometallic Electrolyte Additive
paper.abstract: Despite the high theoretical capacity of sodium metal anodes, practical application is limited by the general instability of the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) leading to dendritic growth and capacity fade. Here we report that the dimolybdenum paddlewheel complex, Mo2(mea)4 (1, mea = 2-(2-methoxyethoxy)acetate), functions as an effective electrolyte additive for Na metal anodes at millimolar loadings, enabled by self-assembly on the anode surface upon formation of aggregates involving 1 and Na+. In symmetric Na||Na cells, additive 1 was found to increase cycling stability and attenuate overpotential growth and impedance rise over 450 cycles compared to additive-free controls. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed that 1 promotes early formation of an inorganic-rich SEI that also contains intact 1 and its downstream products. Scanning electron microscopy confirmed suppression of morphologies associated with dendrite growth. Full-cell Na||Na3V2(PO4)3 testing demonstrated improved Coulombic efficiency relative to an additive-free control and served to validate cathode compatibility of the additive. This work establishes organometallic complexes as an effective “third class” of Na metal battery additives, complementing purely organic or inorganic systems.

paper.title: Electrochemical Capture of Microplastics via Reversible Metal Deposition in Aqueous Solutions
paper.abstract: Microplastics are persistent aqueous contaminants for which effective removal strategies remain needed. Here, we investigate electrochemical deposition as a means of capturing suspended polystyrene (PS) particles. The purpose of this study is to understand the plausibility of electrochemical deposition as a means for removing microplastics from aqueous systems. The central hypothesis guiding this work is that ramified solid metallic deposits created during electrodeposition can mechanically capture plastic particles suspended in the liquid phase. PS particles of 200 nm and 250 μm were evaluated in ZnSO4 electrolyte under applied potentials from 0 to −4 V, with surfactant conditions also examined. Electrochemical treatment resulted in visibly reduced turbidity, suggesting a decrease in suspended particle concentration. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) showed particles attached to or incorporated within deposited zinc. Particle capture was not observed at 0 V but was evident under active zinc deposition at −2 V, supporting the role of electrodeposited zinc in particle capture. The observed particle–electrode interactions differed with particle size: larger particles were partially embedded within rough, dendritic zinc deposits, whereas nanoscale particles were densely distributed across the deposited structure. These observations demonstrate the ability of electrodeposition to facilitate particle capture through distinct particle–deposit interactions and support its potential as a tunable approach for investigating microplastic capture in aqueous systems.
